title: The uncanny valley
hook: Robots grow more likeable as they look human, until they look almost human.
peek: In 1970 the Japanese roboticist Masahiro Mori predicted that near-human robots would feel eerie rather than endearing. He drew a graph with a sudden dip, and the idea, the uncanny valley, now shapes how robots, games and animated films are designed.
lede: In 1970 Masahiro Mori, a robotics professor in Tokyo, wrote a short essay for a Japanese magazine called Energy. He suggested that as a machine looks more human, people feel more warmly towards it, but only up to a point. When it gets very close to human without quite arriving, the warmth drops sharply into unease. On his graph, that dip looks like a valley.

bullets.text: Mori's Japanese phrase was bukimi no tani, roughly a valley of eeriness. The English name uncanny valley spread after the writer Jasia Reichardt used it in her 1978 book about robots.
Mori argued that motion makes the effect stronger. A realistic artificial hand might pass for real while still, but once it moves slightly wrongly, the impression breaks and the unease grows.

Rather than chase perfect realism, Mori advised robot designers to aim for the first peak before the valley: clearly a machine, but a pleasant one. Many friendly robots and cartoon characters sit right there.
In 2009 researchers at Princeton found that macaque monkeys looked less at realistic computer-made monkey faces than at real or cartoonish ones, a hint that the reaction is not purely cultural.
Mori offered no experiments, only a thought. Later studies find the dip under some conditions but not others, and researchers still debate what causes it.
